summary: Follow-up plan for Layer DT.0 (heights and approximation constants) of Diophantine approximation and transcendence. The accepted base packet plans the stage's 46 targets (heights of algebraic numbers and their comparisons, Siegel's lemma over a number field, Dirichlet's theorems through Minkowski, Kronecker's theorem, the exponents of approximation, badly approximable numbers and continued fractions); they are cited by id and not planned again. This packet closes what that pass and the consumers of the layer left open. (1) The covering input of Kronecker's theorem, requested from GeometryOfNumbersAndQuadraticArithmetic:GN.4: if every nonzero vector of the polar lattice L* has length at least R, every point lies within n/R of L (Evertse, Corollary 2.21, with the explicit constant n), derived from GN.4's covering transference μ(L)·λ₁(L*) ≤ n, in Euclidean and in maximum-norm form. (2) Siegel's lemma over a number field in product form (Berrevoets, Lemma 3.2), which ClassicalArithmeticCompletion:CA.6 requested for Dobrowolski's auxiliary polynomial: the bound uses the product over rows and embeddings of the embedding maxima rather than a uniform house bound. (3) The characterisation of badly approximable numbers by bounded partial quotients, with explicit constants in both directions, which ProbabilisticAndMetricNumberTheory:PM.4 requested in terms of Mathlib's GenContFract.of. (4) The maximum absolute height of a tuple of algebraic numbers, the convention of Binyamini's point-counting paper routed to this layer (PAPER-BINYAMINI-22/53), with the minimal-polynomial formula for the absolute height as API. No new gaps or requests: the GN.1 promotion bridge of the base packet is obsolete, since the GeometryOfNumbersAndQuadraticArithmetic packet is promoted and its node GN.1/minkowski-linear-forms resolves.

nodes.title: Covering bound from a polar lattice without short vectors
nodes.statement: Let E be a real inner-product space of finite dimension n, let L ⊂ E be a discrete full ℤ-lattice, and let L* = {y ∈ E : ⟨y, x⟩ ∈ ℤ for every x ∈ L} be its polar lattice. Let R > 0 and suppose that ‖y‖ ≥ R for every nonzero y ∈ L*. Then every b ∈ E has a point x ∈ L with ‖x − b‖ ≤ n/R. Coordinate form: let B be an invertible real n × n matrix and L = Bℤⁿ, so that L* = (Bᵀ)⁻¹ℤⁿ for the standard dot product. If every nonzero vector of (Bᵀ)⁻¹ℤⁿ has maximum norm at least R, then for every b ∈ ℝⁿ there is z ∈ ℤⁿ with |(Bz − b)_i| ≤ n/R for every i. This is Evertse's Corollary 2.21 with the explicit constant n in place of n·c(n)/2, and it is the covering input of DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence:DT.0/kronecker-approximation-theorem, applied in ℝ^{n+1} with constant n + 1.
hypotheses: n = dim E may be 0: then E = L = L* = 0, the hypothesis is empty and x = b = 0.
L* is the polar for the inner product that defines ‖·‖. In coordinates the inner product is the standard dot product, and the columns of (Bᵀ)⁻¹ form the basis of L* dual to the columns of B.
The hypothesis bounds the polar lattice from below, not L itself; a lattice without short vectors can cover badly (see the acceptance tests).
Evertse assumes ‖y‖ > R strictly. The non-strict hypothesis suffices here, because the covering transference is applied to the attained first minimum of L*.
proofSteps: If n = 0 take x = 0. Let n ≥ 1. L* is a discrete full lattice: Mathlib's LinearMap.BilinForm.dualSubmodule_span_of_basis identifies it with the ℤ-span of the dual basis, and GeometryOfNumbersAndQuadraticArithmetic:GN.0/covolume-dual records that it is full with covolume covol(L)⁻¹.

The first Euclidean minimum λ₁(L*) of the closed unit ball is at least R: by GeometryOfNumbersAndQuadraticArithmetic:GN.1/successive-minimum-first with r = λ₁(L*), some nonzero y ∈ L* has ‖y‖ ≤ λ₁(L*), and ‖y‖ ≥ R by hypothesis.

GeometryOfNumbersAndQuadraticArithmetic:GN.4/covering-dual-transference gives μ(L)·λ₁(L*) ≤ n for the covering radius μ(L) of GeometryOfNumbersAndQuadraticArithmetic:GN.4/covering-radius, hence μ(L) ≤ n/R.

L is closed in E (a discrete additive subgroup of a Hausdorff topological group: the additive form of Mathlib's Subgroup.isClosed_of_discrete) and nonempty, and E is proper, so IsClosed.exists_infDist_eq_dist gives x ∈ L with ‖x − b‖ = dist(b, L) ≤ μ(L) ≤ n/R.

Coordinate form: take E = EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n) and L the ℤ-span of the columns of B. The columns of (Bᵀ)⁻¹ are the dual basis for the dot product (Evertse §2.4, p. 32), so L* = (Bᵀ)⁻¹ℤⁿ. A vector whose maximum norm is at least R has Euclidean norm at least R, and |(x − b)_i| ≤ ‖x − b‖ (PiLp.norm_apply_le); apply the Euclidean form.
acceptance: Evertse's Theorem 2.20 has an unspecified constant c(n) (his remark offers (4/3)^{n(n−1)/2} or 4ⁿ·vol(Bₙ)⁻²) and Corollary 2.21 the radius n·c(n)/(2R). Through the covering transference μ(L)·λ₁(L*) ≤ n the radius is n/R, with no successive-minima constant.
n = 1, L = aℤ with a > 0: L* = a⁻¹ℤ, the hypothesis holds with R = 1/a, and the theorem gives distance at most a; the true covering radius is a/2.
L = ℤⁿ: L* = ℤⁿ and R = 1; the point (1/2, …, 1/2) is at Euclidean distance √n/2 ≤ n and at maximum-norm distance 1/2 from ℤⁿ.

Swapping L and L* in the hypothesis is false: for n = 2 and L = ℤ × kℤ (k ≥ 2) every nonzero vector of L has length at least 1, yet (0, k/2) is at distance k/2 from L. Here L* = ℤ × k⁻¹ℤ contains (0, 1/k), so the theorem's hypothesis fails for every R > 1/k.
Kronecker's theorem: in ℝ^{n+1} the constant is n + 1, so R := (n + 1)/ε puts every point within Euclidean, hence coordinatewise, distance ε of the lattice L_M of the proof of Evertse's Theorem 2.22.

nodes.title: Siegel's lemma over a number field in product form
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field of degree d and σ₁, …, σ_d its embeddings into ℂ. Let M ≥ 0 and N be integers with N > dM, and let a_ij ∈ 𝓞_K (1 ≤ i ≤ M, 1 ≤ j ≤ N) be such that every row (a_i1, …, a_iN) has a nonzero entry. Put P_i := ∏_{k=1}^{d} max_{1≤j≤N} |σ_k(a_ij)|; then P_i ≥ 1. The system Σ_j a_ij x_j = 0 (1 ≤ i ≤ M) has a solution x ∈ ℤ^N ∖ {0} with max_j |x_j| ≤ ((2√2·N)^{dM}·P_1⋯P_M)^{1/(N−dM)}. For M ≥ 1 this bound equals (2√2·N·(P_1⋯P_M)^{1/(dM)})^{dM/(N−dM)}, the form of Berrevoets's Lemma 3.2.
hypotheses: The unknowns are rational integers and the coefficients algebraic integers. The bound sees each row through its own embedding maxima, so one row with large coefficients does not enlarge the contribution of the others.
Every row must have a nonzero entry: a zero row gives P_i = 0 and the bound 0, which no nonzero x meets. A zero row imposes no condition and can be deleted first.
M = 0 is allowed (bound 1, solution e₁); Berrevoets states M ≥ 1.
σ₁, …, σ_d run over all d ring homomorphisms K → ℂ (NumberField.Embeddings.card): each complex embedding appears together with its conjugate.
proofSteps: Real coordinates: τ_k := σ_k for the r₁ real embeddings and, for one embedding σ of each conjugate pair, Re σ and Im σ; there are d of them. For an integer Y ≥ 1 and y ∈ {0, …, Y}^N each τ_k(Σ_j a_ij y_j) lies in [−A_ki, A_ki] with A_ki := N·Y·max_j |τ_k(a_ij)| ≤ N·Y·max_j |σ_k(a_ij)|.

Cut each interval [−A_ki, A_ki] into n_i equal pieces, n_i := ⌊1 + 2√2·N·Y·P_i^{1/d}⌋, giving ∏_i n_i^d boxes. If (Y + 1)^N > ∏_i n_i^d, the box principle (Finset.exists_ne_map_eq_of_card_lt_of_maps_to) gives y ≠ y′ in one box, and x := y − y′ is nonzero with |x_j| ≤ Y.

Each |τ_k(Σ_j a_ij x_j)| is at most 2A_ki/n_i. Combining the real and imaginary parts of a complex embedding costs a factor √2, so |σ_k(Σ_j a_ij x_j)| ≤ 2√2·N·Y·max_j|σ_k(a_ij)|/n_i for every k (conjugate embeddings have equal absolute values). Multiplying over k gives |N_{K/ℚ}(Σ_j a_ij x_j)| ≤ (2√2·N·Y·P_i^{1/d}/n_i)^d < 1 by the choice of n_i.

The norm of an algebraic integer is a rational integer (Algebra.coe_norm_int) and is the product of the d conjugates (Algebra.norm_eq_prod_embeddings); it vanishes only at 0 (Algebra.norm_eq_zero_iff), and a nonzero integer has absolute value at least 1 (Int.one_le_abs). Hence Σ_j a_ij x_j = 0 for every i.

Counting: a nonzero entry a_iℓ has |N(a_iℓ)| ≥ 1, so P_i ≥ ∏_k |σ_k(a_iℓ)| ≥ 1 and 1 < 2√2·N·P_i^{1/d}. Then n_i < 2√2·N·(Y + 1)·P_i^{1/d}, and the box condition holds as soon as (Y + 1)^{N−dM} ≥ (2√2·N)^{dM}·∏_i P_i. Take Y := ⌊((2√2·N)^{dM}·∏_i P_i)^{1/(N−dM)}⌋, which is at least 1 because the base is at least 1 and N − dM ≥ 1; then Y + 1 exceeds the root and Y is at most the stated bound. (Berrevoets takes Y equal to the root itself, which need not be an integer; sourceIssue E602.)
acceptance: K = ℚ(i) (d = 2), M = 1, N = 3, row (1, i, 1 + i): each embedding has row maximum √2, so P_1 = 2 and the bound is ((6√2)²·2)^{1/1} = 144; x = (1, 1, −1) solves 1 + i − (1 + i) = 0 with max|x_j| = 1.

House form: if |σ_k(a_ij)| ≤ A for all i, j, k, then P_i ≤ A^d and the bound is at most (2√2·N·A)^{dM/(N−dM)}, below the (3NA)^{dM/(N−dM)} of DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence:DT.0/siegel-lemma-number-field once zero rows are discarded (discarding lowers M). The product form refines that node.

K = ℚ: P_i = max_j |a_ij| and the bound ((2√2·N)^M·∏_i max_j |a_ij|)^{1/(N−M)} uses each row's own size, where Mathlib's Int.Matrix.exists_ne_zero_int_vec_norm_le uses the largest entry of the whole matrix.

Dobrowolski's system (ClassicalArithmeticCompletion:CA.6/dobrowolski-auxiliary-polynomial): the rows a_ij = C(j, i)·α^{j−i} (0 ≤ i < M, 0 ≤ j ≤ N, so N + 1 unknowns) contain a_ii = 1, and P_i ≤ N^{d·i}·M(α)^N for an algebraic integer α, which is the input of that node's bound.

uses.where: Berrevoets, proof of Lemma 4.8, printed p. 17 (ClassicalArithmeticCompletion:CA.6/dobrowolski-auxiliary-polynomial)
uses.how: the auxiliary polynomial F with α a zero of multiplicity M has integer coefficients bounded through the product of the embedding maxima, which turns into M(α)^{MN}
the uniform-house form follows by bounding each P_i by A^d

sources.match: The statement: a number field of degree d, algebraic-integer coefficients with no zero row, N > dM, and the bound on max|x_i| through the product over rows and embeddings of the maximal absolute values, with the constant 2√2·N.

sources.locator: Chapter 3, proof of Lemma 3.2, printed pp. 12–15
sources.match: The box principle in the real coordinates τ_k, the choice of n_i through the d-th root of the product, the norm argument, and the choice of Y; followed in the proof steps, with the corrections of E601 and E602.
Why a nonzero solution exists at all: the system is equivalent to dM linear equations over ℚ in N > dM unknowns.
The uniform-house form (3NA)^{dM/(N−dM)}, which the product form refines.

nodes.title: Badly approximable numbers are those with bounded partial quotients
nodes.statement: Let ξ be an irrational real number with simple continued fraction ξ = [a₀; a₁, a₂, …]. In Mathlib's form, a_{n+1} is the n-th partial denominator of GenContFract.of ξ: (GenContFract.of ξ).partDens.get? n = some a_{n+1} for every n ≥ 0. Write ‖t‖ = |t − round t|. (a) If a_n ≤ B for every n ≥ 1, then q·‖qξ‖ > 1/(B + 2) for every integer q ≥ 1. (b) If c > 0 and q·‖qξ‖ ≥ c for every integer q ≥ 1, then a_n ≤ 1/c for every n ≥ 1. Consequently ξ is badly approximable (DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence:DT.0/badly-approximable) if and only if its partial quotients a₁, a₂, … are bounded.
hypotheses: ξ irrational. A rational number has a terminating expansion, so its partial quotients are trivially bounded, but DT.0/badly-approximable excludes rationals: the equivalence fails without irrationality.
a₀ = ⌊ξ⌋ is not a partial denominator and is not bounded by B; it is an arbitrary integer.

Pottmeyer defines badly approximable by liminf q²·|ξ − p/q| > 0 over coprime (p, q) with q ≥ 1. His definition admits rationals; for irrational ξ it agrees with DT.0/badly-approximable, since q·‖qξ‖ = q²·|ξ − p/q| for p the integer nearest to qξ.
For 0 < ξ < 1 the a_n (n ≥ 1) are the digits of the Gauss map, the form used by ProbabilisticAndMetricNumberTheory:PM.4.
proofSteps: Notation: q_n := (GenContFract.of ξ).dens n and p_n the numerators. As ξ is irrational the expansion does not terminate (GenContFract.terminates_iff_rat), so partDens.get? n = some a_{n+1} for every n, with a_{n+1} ≥ 1 an integer (GenContFract.of_one_le_get?_partDen, GenContFract.exists_int_eq_of_partDen). The p_n and q_n are integers, q_n ≥ 1, and p_n/q_n = ξ.convergent n (Real.convs_eq_convergent).
(b) GenContFract.abs_sub_convergents_le' gives |ξ − p_n/q_n| ≤ 1/(a_{n+1}·q_n²). With q = q_n: c ≤ q_n·‖q_nξ‖ ≤ q_n·|q_nξ − p_n| ≤ 1/a_{n+1}, so a_{n+1} ≤ 1/c.

(a) Let q ≥ 1 and p := round(qξ). If q·‖qξ‖ ≥ 1/2 we are done, since B ≥ 1 gives 1/2 > 1/(B + 2). Otherwise r := p/q satisfies |ξ − r| = ‖qξ‖/q < 1/(2q²) ≤ 1/(2·den(r)²), so Legendre's theorem (Real.exists_rat_eq_convergent) gives r = ξ.convergent k for some k, with den(r) = q_k ≤ q.

DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence:DT.0/convergent-error-lower-bound gives |ξ − r| > 1/(q_k(q_k + q_{k+1})). The recurrence q_{k+1} = a_{k+1}·q_k + q_{k−1} (GenContFract.dens_recurrence, with q_{−1} = 0) and q_{k−1} ≤ q_k (GenContFract.of_den_mono) give q_{k+1} ≤ (B + 1)·q_k. Hence ‖qξ‖ = q·|ξ − r| > q/((B + 2)·q_k²) ≥ 1/((B + 2)·q).
The equivalence: (a) with c = 1/(B + 2) shows that bounded partial quotients make ξ badly approximable, and (b) bounds the partial quotients of a badly approximable ξ by 1/c.
acceptance: Golden ratio φ = [1; 1, 1, …]: (a) gives q·‖qφ‖ > 1/3 for every q ≥ 1; the true liminf is 1/√5 ≈ 0.447 (Hurwitz), consistent with the bound.
√2 = [1; 2, 2, …]: (a) gives q·‖q√2‖ > 1/4; at q = 1, 2, 5, 12 the values are about 0.414, 0.343, 0.355 and 0.353. Conversely (b) with c = 1/4 bounds the partial quotients by 4.
ξ = 1/2: GenContFract.of (1/2) has the single partial denominator 2, so its partial denominators are bounded, yet 2·‖2·(1/2)‖ = 0 and 1/2 is not badly approximable: irrationality is needed.
liouvilleNumber 10 is not badly approximable (a unit test of DT.0/badly-approximable), so its partial quotients are unbounded.

nodes.title: The maximum absolute height of a tuple of algebraic numbers
nodes.statement: Let F be a field of characteristic zero, ι a finite type and y : ι → F. Define h_max(y) := max_{i∈ι} h(y_i), where h = NumberField.absLogHeight₁ is the absolute logarithmic Weil height, with h_max(y) := 0 when ι is empty; in Lean this is the real supremum ⨆ i, absLogHeight₁ (y i), which is 0 for an empty family. Its multiplicative form is H_max(y) := exp h_max(y), the maximum of 1 and the absMulHeight₁(y_i). For an algebraic x of degree d whose primitive minimal polynomial is a₀·∏_{i=1}^{d}(X − x_i) with a₀ > 0, h(x) = (log a₀ + Σ_i log max(1, |x_i|))/d.
hypotheses: F has characteristic zero. A transcendental coordinate gets Mathlib's junk value h = 0, so statements about the height of a tuple assume every coordinate algebraic.

This is the maximum of the scalar heights, not the absolute height of the projective point [1 : y_1 : ⋯ : y_m]. The projective tuple height and its comparison with h_max belong to HeightsRationalPointsAndObstructions:RP.0.
proofSteps: Define maxAbsLogHeight y := ⨆ i, NumberField.absLogHeight₁ (y i) in ℝ. The family is finite, hence bounded, and Real.iSup_of_isEmpty gives the value 0 for empty ι.

Nonnegativity: for algebraic x, absMulHeight₁ x is mulHeight₁ of the generator of ℚ(x), which is at least 1 (Height.one_le_mulHeight₁), raised to a positive power; otherwise it is 1. So absLogHeight₁ x ≥ 0, and h_max(y) ≥ 0.

The formula for h(x): DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence:DT.0/height-comparisons gives log M(x) = d·h(x), and DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence:DT.0/mahler-measure-of-algebraic-number gives M(x) = a₀·∏_i max(1, |x_i|).

Invariance: h(x) depends only on the minimal polynomial of x (DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence:DT.0/abs-mul-height-eq-of-minpoly-eq), so h_max is unchanged by a field embedding applied to every coordinate and by reindexing.

Northcott: for fixed m and D, the tuples in ℂ^m of algebraic numbers of degree at most D with h_max ≤ T form a finite set, coordinate by coordinate from DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence:DT.0/northcott-absolute-height.
acceptance: h_max of the empty tuple is 0, and h_max(i, −1) = 0 (roots of unity).
h_max(2, 1/2) = log 2, while the projective point [1 : 2 : 1/2] = [2 : 4 : 1] has logarithmic height log 4: the two notions differ.

the lower bound for an integer polynomial at an algebraic point is stated through H(y)^{d(m+1)} with H(y) = exp h_max(y)

api.name: DiophantineApproximation.maxAbsLogHeight
api.statement: h_max(y) := ⨆ i, absLogHeight₁(y_i) for y : ι → F with ι finite.

api.name: DiophantineApproximation.maxAbsLogHeight_unique
api.statement: For ι with exactly one element i, h_max(y) = absLogHeight₁(y_i).

api.name: DiophantineApproximation.maxAbsLogHeight_le_iff
api.statement: For t ≥ 0: h_max(y) ≤ t if and only if absLogHeight₁(y_i) ≤ t for every i.

api.name: DiophantineApproximation.absLogHeight₁_nonneg
api.statement: 0 ≤ absLogHeight₁ x for every x in a field of characteristic zero, since absMulHeight₁ x ≥ 1.

api.name: DiophantineApproximation.maxAbsLogHeight_comp_equiv
api.statement: h_max(y ∘ e) = h_max(y) for an equivalence e : κ ≃ ι.

api.name: DiophantineApproximation.maxAbsLogHeight_map
api.statement: h_max(f ∘ y) = h_max(y) for a ring homomorphism f : F → F′ of characteristic-zero fields; f maps algebraic elements to algebraic elements of the same minimal polynomial and transcendental ones to transcendental ones.

api.name: DiophantineApproximation.absLogHeight₁_eq_log_mahlerMeasure_div
api.statement: For algebraic x of degree d: absLogHeight₁ x = log M(x)/d = (log a₀ + Σ_i log max(1, |x_i|))/d (Binyamini's formula (1)).

api.name: DiophantineApproximation.maxAbsMulHeight_eq_max_one_iSup
api.statement: H_max(y) = max(1, max_i absMulHeight₁(y_i)); in particular H_max of the empty tuple is 1.

api.name: DiophantineApproximation.finite_setOf_maxAbsLogHeight_le
api.statement: For m, D ∈ ℕ and T ∈ ℝ, the set of y ∈ ℂ^m with every y_i algebraic of degree at most D and h_max(y) ≤ T is finite (Northcott for tuples).

tests.name: DiophantineApproximation.test_maxAbsLogHeight_empty
tests.statement: maxAbsLogHeight y = 0 for y : Fin 0 → ℚ.

tests.name: DiophantineApproximation.test_maxAbsLogHeight_sqrtTwo
tests.statement: maxAbsLogHeight ![√2] = (log 2)/2; the height of √2 computed in ℚ(√2) without the 1/[ℚ(√2):ℚ] normalisation would give log 2.

tests.name: DiophantineApproximation.test_maxAbsLogHeight_ne_projective
tests.statement: maxAbsLogHeight ![(2 : ℚ), 1/2] = log 2, whereas the projective point [1 : 2 : 1/2] = [2 : 4 : 1] has Height.logHeight ![(2 : ℚ), 4, 1] = log 4.

sources.match: The absolute logarithmic Weil height through the minimal polynomial over ℤ, h(x) = (log|a₀| + Σ log⁺|x_i|)/d, H = e^h, and the height of a vector as the largest height of its coordinates.

sourceIssues.locator: Chapter 3, proof of Lemma 3.2, printed p. 14 (PDF p. 15), the justification of the strict inequality in the count of boxes
sourceIssues.printed: For a nonzero entry a_iℓ of row i the source asserts that the d-th root of ∏_k |σ_k(a_iℓ)| equals |N_{K/ℚ}(a_iℓ)|, and concludes that it is at least 1.
sourceIssues.correction: The d-th root of ∏_k |σ_k(a_iℓ)| is |N_{K/ℚ}(a_iℓ)|^{1/d}. It is still at least 1, because the norm of a nonzero algebraic integer is a nonzero rational integer, so the conclusion stands.
sourceIssues.reason: ∏_k |σ_k(a)| over the d embeddings is |N_{K/ℚ}(a)| itself. For K = ℚ(i) and a = 2 the product is 4 = N(2), and its square root is 2, not 4.

sourceIssues.locator: Chapter 3, proof of Lemma 3.2, printed pp. 12 and 14 (PDF pp. 13 and 15), the choice of Y
sourceIssues.printed: The box principle is set up for a positive integer Y, with y ranging over {0, …, Y}^N (p. 12); at the end Y is set equal to the real number ((2√2N)^{dM}·∏_i∏_k max_j|σ_k(a_ij)|)^{1/(N−dM)} (p. 14).
sourceIssues.correction: Take Y to be the integer part of that root. The root is at least 1, so Y ≥ 1; Y + 1 exceeds the root, so condition (12) and hence (10) hold; and Y is at most the root, so the bound of Lemma 3.2 holds as stated.
sourceIssues.reason: The pigeonhole step needs the finite set {0, …, Y}^N, which requires an integer Y. Already for K = ℚ, M = 1, N = 2 and the row (1, 1) the root is 4√2 ≈ 5.66.
